messages:
sara: Heads-up — saw memory creeping on prod after a long chat session (>12k tokens). KV pages show entries that look like they belong to previous requests.
mike: Can you paste the quick repro or logs? sounds like cross-request contamination which we thought we fixed last quarter.
sara: Minimal logs — note the slab headers getting re-used when a batch split happens. Repro steps below.

sara: ```
# repro (local with small batch window)
REDWOOD_BATCH_WINDOW_MS=12 ./bin/runtime --model gptx --seq 12288 --send-multi-turn 1
# watch /proc/<pid>/maps and the KV slab pages
```

sara: snippet from kv debug dump (token_offset is wrong — it restarts inside a slab):

sara: ```
KV_PAGE 0x7f8a  slab_id=42  owner_req=1532  tokens=8192  tail_off=4096
entry@4096: req_tag=1531 token_off=0 len=64
entry@4160: req_tag=1531 token_off=64 len=64
entry@4224: req_tag=1532 token_off=0 len=32  <- this should be aligned to 8192 boundary
```

anna: That entry@4224 having req_tag=1532 but token_off=0 inside same slab looks wrong. Could be a batch-split write that never updated the slab base offset after a kernel-chosen split.
jorge: Related: I toggled a new batching heuristic yesterday (split_on_seq_boundary=true) which also flips the runtime kernel selection to the 'small-kernel' path for the trailing fragment. Possibly two things interacting.

mike: Bench results? bench-bot, do we have the profile traces from the 02:10 deploy that enabled the heuristic?
bench-bot: Uploaded profile -> s3://redwood-perf/profiles/1765431200-split-heuristic.tar.gz
mike: Thanks. I looked quickly — there's a spike in the KV writer lock stall around the batch boundary and a context switch surge when small-kernel path is chosen.

anna: Hypothesis: when a batch split occurs the writer code switches to a different allocation strategy (fast-path slab append vs append-with-header). The fast-path reuses an existing slab pointer without advancing the 'slab_base_token' for the new request, so token offsets get interpreted relative to the prior request.
sara: That would explain both stale blocks (old req_tag present) and wrong token alignment. Also explains memory growth because those partly-overwritten entries never get tombstoned and aren't evicted due to incorrect keys.
jorge: Quick mitigation: make the batch-split atomic w.r.t. slab allocation: allocate a new slab and zero header before any writes. Also add per-request sentinel (request_uuid) in the slab header and validate on read.

mike: Can we push a small runtime guard to prod: if slab.header.req_uuid != current_req_uuid then treat entries as invalid and force re-alloc + tombstone, and emit a metric kv.slab.contam_detected? low-risk toggle.
anna: I can draft the PR: add guard in kv_read() and kv_write() and a canary flag runtime.env KV_STRICT_GUARD=1. Also adjust the kernel selection benchmark to avoid switching kernel mid-slab until guards are upstreamed.
sara: Another perf note — the kernel selector chooses small-kernel when trailing fragment length < 128 and we have batching enabled. That small kernel path currently uses a different allocator path (fast bump) that doesn't update the slab 'page_offset' atomic. I'll instrument that in the allocator.

jorge: For repro coverage, add a fuzz test that simulates interleaved requests with forced batch splits on sequence boundaries and asserts no cross-request req_tag in any slab.

mike: Priority: P1 for correctness, P2 for perf follow-up. Sara/Anna, please post the PR links and I'll own the canary rollout.
sara: Will do. PR link once ready. For now I'm adding a short-lived alert: kv.slab.contam_detected > 0 -> page on eng-runtime.
anna: PR opened: https://git.redwood/scm/runtime/+/4321-kv-slab-guard
sara: Thanks — I'll coordinate canary and collect heap/dump snapshots after rollout.
mike: Good plan. If we see significant perf regression from the guard, we'll try the tombstone-only path first (mark on read, evict lazily) and then optimize.
jorge: FYI, I'll also check model kernel selection unit tests — we shouldn't change kernel mid-write without ordering fences.

sara: TL;DR: batch-split + kernel path switch -> wrong slab base handling -> stale entries + wrong token offsets -> memory growth after long contexts. Mitigation = strict slab guard + allocate-on-split + test coverage.
